https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text: 1:12 Typhoon Dolphin batters parts of east and south-east Asia – video Extreme weather Typhoon Dolphin: more than a million people evacuated in China as record rainfall dumped on Shanghai Authorities warn that days of intense rain could trigger widespread flooding and landslides as storm moves north and further inland Yu-chen Li in Taipei Mon 10 Aug 2026 00.55 EDT First published on Sun 9 Aug 2026 23.46 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google More than a million people were moved to safety across eastern China by Sunday evening as powerful Typhoon Dolphin made landfall amid fears torrential rain would cause flooding and landslides. Wenzhou, a coastal city in Zhejiang province, said it relocated more than 900,000 people and opened more than 1,500 emergency shelters. In neighbouring Fujian, 98,900 people were moved from high-risk areas. Hong Kong records hottest day ever as Typhoon Dolphin fuels heatwave Read more In Shanghai, 215,600 people were moved from areas considered at risk by Sunday evening, substantially higher than an earlier figure of 30,300. A weather station in central Shanghai recorded nearly 313mm of rain in the 24 hours to 7am on Monday, its highest 24-hour rainfall in more than 150 years of records. Another station in the city recorded nearly 400mm. The hashtag “Shanghai turns into the sea” began trending on the Chinese social media platform Weibo, as videos circulated showing streets flooded around the Wukang Mansion, one of the city’s best-known tourist landmarks. The average rainfall recorded across Zhejiang from Friday evening to Monday morning reached 173mm, reportedly surpassing the levels seen during previous major typhoons including Lekima and Bavi. Dolphin weakened rapidly to a tropical storm by 5am on Monday. But as the storm continued to move northwards and farther inland, heavy rain was forecast across large parts of eastern and central China , extending north into Shandong and affecting Henan, Hubei, Anhui, Jiangsu, Zhejiang and Shanghai. Authorities maintained an orange alert for heavy rain and warned that days of intense rain could trigger widespread flooding and landslides through Wednesday, urging people to stay indoors during the heavy downpours. Forecasters in China predicted some areas could see 200-400mm (7.9–15.7 inches) of rainfall over the coming days. View image in fullscreen A temporary shelter in Hangzhou, where thousands of people were evacuated because of Typhoon Dolphin. Photograph: VCG/Getty Images The storm forced Shanghai’s two airports to cancel more than 1,300 flights. Public transport services, including many local trains, have been suspended in the financial hub. Zhejiang’s Ningbo international airport, about 150km south of Shanghai, will resume flight operations from midday (0400 GMT) on Monday. But the airport warned some journeys may yet be delayed or cancelled. Provincial capital Hangzhou resumed subway services on Monday morning, after halting some train operations on Sunday. Elsewhere, Dolphin fuelled intense heat over Hong Kong on Sunday, pushing the city to its highest ever temperature of 36.9C . The extremely hot weather was expected to continue into Tuesday, officials said. In Taiwan, ferry services were suspended and more than 180 flights were cancelled as the storm brought downpours and strong winds on Sunday. Dolphin earlier swept through Japan’s southern Okinawa prefecture, injuring six people and ⁠cutting power to more than 50,000 buildings. In the Philippines, the typhoon did not make landfall in the country’s north but intensified the seasonal monsoon rains, which flooded many areas of the main northern Luzon region, including around Manila. Scientists say global warming has made extreme weather more likely, including more powerful typhoons. Oficials believe the trip addressed the wars in Ukraine and Iran, as well as NATO’s Article 5 commitments. While acknowledging a rise in Russian hybrid attacks and sabotage across Europe, officials confirmed no changes in Russia’s conventional military posture. by Kyiv Post | Aug. 29, 2026, 2:45 pm Flip Share Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Bluesky Email Copy Copied (LtoR) NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte, German Defence Minister Boris Pistorius, Rheinmetall CEO Armin Papperger and German Finance Minister and Vice Chancellor Lars Klingbeil visit the site of the new munitions plant of German automotive and arms manufactuer Rheinmetall during its inauguration in Unterluess, northern Germany on Aug. 27, 2025. (Photo by Ronny HARTMANN / AFP) Content Share Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Bluesky Email Copy Copied Flip European officials stated there is no evidence that Russia is preparing for a conventional military attack on NATO or the Baltic states, pushing back against reports regarding the primary focus of CIA Director John Ratcliffe’s recent unannounced visit to Moscow . According to Bloomberg , Ratcliffe’s visit likely addressed efforts to end the war in Ukraine, reaffirmed NATO’s Article 5 mutual defense commitments, and covered the ongoing conflict with Iran. JOIN US ON TELEGRAM Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official . Sources indicated that Ratcliffe may have also sought to deter Russian retaliation against US economic measures targeting Iran and to press Moscow to cease its support for Tehran. European officials noted they had not received a formal US briefing on the trip, basing their assessments on independent intelligence and historical US operating procedures. Advertisement While noting that maintaining intelligence channels with Russia is routine, sources told Bloomberg it was notable that Ratcliffe appeared to want the visit made public. The officials acknowledged a rise in Russian hybrid operations, including assassination attempts, sabotage, and airspace incursions, noting that Europe has largely been unprepared for the incidents. However, they stressed that recent intelligence shows no shift in Russia’s conventional military posture that would indicate an impending attack. To mitigate the risk of miscalculation amid the growing hybrid threats, NATO allies have reportedly been discussing how to enhance intelligence and military engagement with Russia. Other Topics of Interest Polish PM Tusk Warns of Russian Escalation in Coming Months Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk stated that Russia is actively preparing for an escalation of tension during the upcoming autumn and winter. Tusk warns of regional escalation The European officials’ assessments contrast with recent warnings from Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk, who stated on Friday, Aug. 28, that Russia is actively preparing for further escalation. Speaking in Olsztyn, Tusk described the upcoming autumn and winter as critical for the security of Ukraine , Poland, and the wider region. Addressing Ratcliffe’s Moscow trip, Tusk noted that Warsaw was not surprised due to its constant coordination with the CIA, though he emphasized that the current security situation extends well beyond the scope of the intelligence director’s visit. Advertisement Tusk’s stark security warning comes days after Polish and Ukrainian leaders exchanged public messages reaffirming their bilateral ties amid the ongoing war. Ukrainian officials confirmed the receipt of an Independence Day letter from Polish President Karol Nawrocki to President Volodymyr Zelensky, in which Nawrocki wished Ukraine victory in its existential struggle against Russia and the full restoration of its internationally recognized borders. https://www.dw.com/en/north-korea-expels.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5Pr0a Prefer DW on Google Swiss Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis met his North Korean counterpart, Choe Son Hui, in Pyongyang in October to discuss normalizing diplomatic relations [FILE: October 30, 2026] Image: KCNA/KNS/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement North Korea has declared Switzerland 's top diplomatic representative in Pyongyang persona non grata and ordered him to leave the country within 48 hours, state media reported on Wednesday. The North Korean Foreign Ministry also called for the closure of Switzerland's diplomatic office in the capital, less than a month after it reopened following a lengthy shutdown during the COVID-19 pandemic. Swiss Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis met with senior North Korean ruling party official Jo Yong Won during his visit to Pyongyang in October [FILE: October 30, 2026] Image: KCNA/KNS/AP Photo/picture alliance According to the state-run Korean Central News Agency (KCNA), Pak Hyon Su, director general of the ministry's European Department, summoned Swiss diplomat Sylvain Astier and handed him a memorandum demanding the office's closure. Pyongyang said the decision was in response to Switzerland's sanctions against a North Korean children's camp, describing the move as an openly hostile act. "Any act of violating the sovereign rights of the DPRK and the interests of its citizens can never be welcomed by us," KCNA reported, using the acronym for North Korea's official name. Why did Switzerland impose sanctions on North Korea? Switzerland placed the Songdowon International Children's Camp in the coastal city of Wonsan under sanctions on November 4. Swiss authorities accused the camp, which also hosts Chinese and Russian students, of participating in the "transfer of Ukrainian children from temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine" to North Korea. They also said the facility contributed to "efforts aimed at the ideological conditioning and russification of Ukrainian children". Kim Yo Jong, the influential sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, condemned the Swiss sanctions [FILE: August 10, 2022] Image: Korean Central News Agency/Korea News Service/AP Photo/picture alliance On Tuesday, Kim Yo Jong, the influential sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un , condemned the sanctions arguing that the measures violated North Korea's sovereignty by interfering with its responsibility to provide children with cultural and recreational opportunities. How has Switzerland responded to North Korea's decision? Switzerland's Foreign Ministry said on Tuesday that reopening its diplomatic office was independent of its sanctions policy. "The reopening of the Swiss diplomatic office in Pyongyang is in line with our universalist foreign policy. Its aim is to maintain channels of dialogue, including with states with which we have differences on certain issues," the ministry said. It stressed that this approach applied regardless of Switzerland's participation in UN sanctions over North Korea's nuclear program or EU sanctions related to Russia's war against Ukraine . Swiss authorities were not immediately available for further comment on Wednesday. South Korea proposes talks to officially end war with North To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Switzerland has maintained diplomatic relations with North Korea since 1974 and has long served as an intermediary between Pyongyang and Western countries. Its office in the North Korean capital closed during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020. Swiss Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis formally reopened it during a visit in October, when he discussed normalizing relations. It was the first visit by a Swiss government minister to North Korea since 2003. The office operates under the Swiss Embassy in Beijing, which handles diplomatic and consular relations with North Korea. Pyongyang also maintains an embassy in Bern. Only a few European countries have diplomatic missions in North Korea, including Sweden , Poland and the Czech Republic . What does North Korea's move mean for relations with the West? Experts say the expulsion is intended as a warning to other Western countries, including the United States , which has been seeking to reestablish contact with Pyongyang. "North Korea is using Switzerland as a test case to show that sanctions and dialogue are incompatible," Lim Eul-chul, a professor at South Korea's Kyungnam University, told news agency Reuters. North Korean leader Kim Jong Un has expressed a willingness to expand diplomatic ties with countries that respect North Korea's sovereignty [FILE: October 23, 2026] Image: KCNA/KNS/AFP Ahn Chan-il, a researcher originally from North Korea, told agency AFP that Pyongyang, backed by its allies China and Russia , wanted to make an example of Switzerland. Earlier this week, North Korean leader Kim Jong Un personally received credentials from the new ambassadors of 10 countries, including Russia and Sweden, in a rare diplomatic ceremony. Kim said Pyongyang was seeking to expand relations with countries that respected its sovereignty but would oppose attempts to restrict the rights and development of sovereign states.
